blocks.title: <ico-book></ico-book> BETWEEN THE LINES
blocks.intro: You already speak in metaphors: you spend time, defend an opinion and digest bad news. This lesson makes the habit conscious, so that you can choose an image, keep it going, and tell a fresh one from a tired one.

vocab.sp: saying one thing is another: «the city is an orchestra»
a comparison with like or as: «like an orchestra»
the picture a metaphor or simile puts in your mind
to keep one image going over several sentences
two images that fight each other in one sentence
an image used so often that nobody sees it anymore
what an orchestra does before it plays: each instrument finds its note
not on the right note; figuratively, not fitting in
to cook gently, just below boiling
to reach boiling point; figuratively, to become exciting (Vera's British form; in US English, «come to a boil»)

blocks.note: How it works: the reading comes first , then flashcards , compare , gap-fill , memory and a conversation with a critic. Every option is grammatical; choose the one that keeps the image whole.

parts.html: 1 · THE METAPHORS YOU ALREADY LIVE BY — four families hidden in everyday English

items.en: She defended her position and attacked mine.
I spent an hour on it. Don't waste my time.
That plan is half-baked, but it's food for thought.
He is at a crossroads. She has come a long way.

parts.html: 2 · SIMILE OR METAPHOR — one compares, the other claims

items.en: The lobby was like an aquarium.
items.sp: Simile: the comparison is announced. Careful, clear, a little cooler.
Metaphor: no warning. Stronger, and it asks the reader to do the work.

parts.html: 3 · EXTEND IT, DON'T MIX IT — stay inside one picture

items.en: The city is an orchestra. The buses are its brass, and the rain keeps time.
items.sp: Extended: every new detail comes from the same picture.

items.en: We need to iron out the bottlenecks.
items.sp: Mixed: nobody irons a bottle. Two images collide, and the reader laughs in the wrong place.

parts.html: 4 · DEAD, TIRED, FRESH — the life cycle of an image

items.en: We camped at the foot of the mountain.
items.sp: Dead: nobody pictures a foot. It is simply vocabulary now, and perfectly fine.

items.en: It was a rollercoaster of emotions.
items.sp: A cliché: everybody has heard it, nobody feels it. Cut it or replace it.
Fresh: you have not read it before, and you can hear it.

parts.html: 5 · HEADLINE PUNS — find the word with two jobs

items.en: Local bakery rises to the occasion.
items.sp: Rises: the bakery succeeds, and bread rises.

items.en: Orchestra strike: talks end on a sour note.
items.sp: A sour note: a wrong note in music, and a bad ending to a meeting.

parts.body: To decode a headline pun, ask which word belongs both to the story and to the subject. Editors choose it on purpose; the second meaning is the joke.

parts.html: CALQUE ALERT — images that do not travel

items.en: They spared no expense on the gala.
items.sp: Some Spanish images make no sense in English. Nobody here «throws the house through the window»; they spare no expense, or go all out.
And nobody has «hairs on the tongue». When an image does not cross, translate the meaning and look for the English picture.

items.en: We'll cross that bridge when we come to it.
items.sp: Watch for mixed images when you half-remember an idiom: you cross this bridge; you do not burn it when you get to it.

blocks.title: <ico-star></ico-star> BETWEEN THE LINES
blocks.intro: Eight o'clock in the hotel library. Sol, now happily installed in her silent room on the sixth floor, reads from her new novel to forty guests. In the front row, with a notebook and a very sharp pencil, sits Vera, the critic. You are at the back, by the door, in case anyone needs anything. Nobody does. Everyone is listening.

cast.sp: reads a page built on a single image
the critic: she will answer in images of her own
by the door, reading between the lines

blocks.title: AUDIO 1 · THE READING
blocks.desc: Sol reads from chapter three. Her character, Ines, has come back to her city after eleven years and cannot sleep. Follow the one image that runs through the whole page, and notice the moment a second image slips in.

questions.q: What does the central metaphor compare?
options: The sounds of the city at night to an orchestra tuning up
Ines to the conductor of an orchestra
The hotel to a concert hall

questions.q: How does Sol extend the image?
options: She describes the weather in more and more detail
Each street sound becomes an instrument or a section: strings, drums, woodwinds, brass
She repeats the word "orchestra" in every sentence

questions.q: "Out of tune. Not the city. Me." What does Ines mean?
options: The city has become noisy and ugly
She has forgotten how to play her instrument
She no longer fits into the life of the city

questions.q: What is the mood of the passage?
options: Wistful, with a touch of dry humor at the end

speaking.prompt: Add one more instrument to Sol's orchestra. Describe a sound from your own street at night as part of the music, in two sentences.
speaking.starter: Then the (instrument) came in: (the sound from your street)…

transcript.html: Thank you. This is from the third chapter. Ines has come back to the city after eleven years, and she cannot sleep.

At night the city did not go quiet. It tuned up. From the ninth floor she could hear it finding its note: a tram dragging its bow along the avenue, slow and low, and somewhere beneath it the kettledrum of a delivery truck taking a corner too fast. The traffic lights kept time for nobody. Green, amber, red. Green, amber, red. A conductor rehearsing in an empty hall.

She opened the window. The woodwinds came in first, as they always had: the thin whistle of the bakery's fan, the cough of a shutter going up. Then the brass, a motorbike three streets away, showing off. Every instrument was where she had left it. She could have written out the score from memory.

And yet she could not find her own part. Eleven years ago, she had known exactly where to come in. She had walked these streets on the beat, late for everything and somehow always on time. Now she stood at the window like a musician who has turned up for the wrong concert, holding an instrument nobody had asked for. The city played on, perfectly, without her. It had not replaced her. That would have been something. It had simply closed the gap, the way water closes over a stone.
Out of tune, she thought. Not the city. Me.

Below, a street sweeper began his long, soft solo, brushing the night toward the gutter. She listened until he reached the end of the block. Then, very quietly, so as not to disturb the orchestra, she hummed one note, just to see whether anything would answer.
A dog did. It was not the answer she had hoped for. But it was, she had to admit, an answer. Thank you.

pair.b: The second chapter never comes to the boil.

items.q: In B, what is it that never happens?

items.q: Which family of metaphor does B belong to?

options: The plot simmers for a hundred pages and then boils over.

items.q: Which image is fresh, not a cliché?

blocks.title: KEEP THE IMAGE WHOLE
blocks.intro: Each sentence has started a picture. Choose the word that comes from the same picture. The other two are good English from the wrong family.

items.q: The debate was a battle: she defended her position and ___ his.
Time is money in this office, so don't ___ it.
The idea was half-baked, so I told him to put it back in the ___.
After the divorce he was at a crossroads, unsure which ___ to take.
The city is an orchestra, and the rain keeps ___.
The first chapter simmers; the second never comes to the ___.
She has come a long way, and there is still a long ___ ahead.
His argument was a house of cards: one question, and it ___.

blocks.title: KEEP VERA'S METAPHOR GOING
blocks.intro: After the reading, Vera turns to you. She talks about the book as cooking. One reply stays in her kitchen, one mixes in a different image, and one is plain and flat. Stay in the kitchen.

lines.html: The opening simmers nicely, don't you think?

options: It does. It really hits the ground running.
It does. She lets it heat slowly.
Yes. It is a good opening.

lines.html: But I'm not sure the middle ever comes to the boil.

options: Perhaps she turned the heat down on purpose.
Perhaps the train left the rails there.

lines.html: And that stone in the water, in the middle of all the music. One ingredient too many?

options: Yes. It was the last nail in the coffin.
Yes. I noticed that sentence too.
A pinch too much, perhaps. The dish was already seasoned.
A sharp little taste to finish. It cuts the sweetness.
It really knocks it out of the park.
I'd go back for a second helping.
It's a home run that hits all the right notes.

blocks.title: AUDIO 2 · THE REVIEW
blocks.desc: Later that night, Vera dictates her notes for Monday's column. The review is itself made of images. Decide: is it a good review? And which family is she cooking with?

options: No: she finds nothing to praise
Mostly: she admires the craft, criticizes two things and expects more
Yes: it is praise from start to finish

questions.q: Which family of metaphor does Vera use all the way through?
What does she criticize with "one spice too many"?
options: The slow middle of the chapter
The image of the stone and the water, which does not belong with the music

questions.q: "Three stars, and a fourth on the table, waiting." What does this mean?
options: She may give a fourth star if the rest of the book delivers
She has given the book four stars
She took one star away at the last minute

speaking.prompt: Review the last film or series you watched in three sentences, all inside one family of metaphor: food, war or a journey.
speaking.starter: The first half… (one image). The second half… (same family). In the end,… (same family).

transcript.html: Notes for Monday's column. Sol read a chapter of her new novel last night, in the hotel library, to forty people and one critic. The opening simmers. She adds her ingredients slowly, a tram here, a bakery there, and by the end of the page the whole city is on the stove. It is patient cooking, and I admired it.

The middle, I am sorry to say, never comes to the boil. The heroine stands at a window, and stands, and stands. I began to wish someone would turn up the heat, or at least open the oven door. And one image is overseasoned: in the middle of all that music, a stone drops into water. One spice too many.

But then comes the last line, with the dog, and it is perfectly judged: a sharp, dry finish that sends you back for more. So. Is it a feast? Not yet. It is an excellent first course, served by a cook who knows exactly what she is doing and is in no hurry to tell us. I shall stay for the main dish. Three stars, and a fourth on the table, waiting.

blocks.title: <ico-pen></ico-pen> MY CITY AS…
blocks.intro: Describe your own city, or your neighborhood, through one extended metaphor of your choice: a kitchen, a ship, a theater, a body, a machine, an animal (about 100 words). Not an orchestra: that one is taken.
checklist: One image, announced in the first or second sentence
Extended at least three times: three details that all come from the same picture
No mixing: nothing from a second picture slips in
No clichés from this lesson (rollercoaster of emotions, at the end of the day, the city that never sleeps)
One simile or one fresh image that is entirely yours
blocks.example: My city is your image. a place in the city is its a part of the image, and the people or the traffic a verb from the same picture. At night, a third detail from the same picture. As for me, I am your own place inside the image.
blocks.hw: Write your description, then record yourself reading it slowly, the way Sol read hers. Send me the text and the audio on WhatsApp.

rubric.d: About 100 words about a real place, built on one image from the first sentence to the last.
The metaphor is extended at least three times without mixing, and there is not a cliché in it.
A reader can see the place and the image at the same time, and nothing has to be explained.
